pm9_israel.topic: Israel's own spending on influence abroad

claims.text: Israel's 2026 budget includes about $730M for public diplomacy, more than four times the roughly $150M of 2025, which was itself about twenty times the pre-war level; Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar compared it to 'investing in jets, bombs and missile interceptors'.

In 2025 Israel's spending included a $50M social-media ad buy (Google, YouTube, X, Outbrain), about $40M to host 400 foreign delegations of lawmakers, pastors, influencers and university presidents, a $4.1M campaign aimed at evangelical churches and the Esther Project influencer network.

The Quincy Institute estimates Israel has likely spent more than $1 billion on public diplomacy since 7 October 2023, including more than $100M in FARA-registered spending; it puts Clock Tower X's contract at $46.5M over one year and lists other registered contracts (Show Faith by Works $3.2M aimed at evangelicals; Israel365; SKDK); it counts 300 Foreign Ministry delegations with 6,000 participants from 70 countries in 2025.

Experts quoted by JTA, including Nicholas Cull (USC), Shibley Telhami (University of Maryland) and Ilan Manor (Ben-Gurion University), argued that messaging cannot overcome objections to policy; Israel's consul general in Los Angeles defended the spending.

claims.text: Declassified UK counted about 180 of 650 MPs in the 2019–24 Parliament funded by pro-Israel groups, individuals or Israeli state institutions, worth over £1M, including over 240 paid trips to Israel costing over £500,000; by party 130 Conservative, 41 Labour, 3 Liberal Democrat, 3 DUP; Conservative Friends of Israel funded 118 sitting Tory MPs on 160 trips (over £330,000); 32 Labour MPs had Labour Friends of Israel-funded trips (over £64,000); over 40 MPs had funding from Israeli state institutions.
Trevor Chinn gave £50,000 to Keir Starmer's 2020 Labour leadership campaign and financed eight members of his front bench; seven members of Starmer's cabinet accepted LFI-funded trips to Israel.

A UK parliamentary petition calling for an inquiry into Israeli state-linked and pro-Israel lobbying, started 28 January 2026, gained 118,306 signatures and was scheduled for debate on 22 June 2026; the Labour government said on 17 April that existing frameworks already provide transparency.

E-petition 752646, created by Andy Kalil, was debated in Westminster Hall on 22 June 2026; John Lamont (Conservative) opened for the Petitions Committee and said he did not support it, arguing it singled out one country and echoed antisemitic claims of Jewish control, and that the clearest documented foreign-influence concerns involved Russia and China; no vote is taken in such debates.

The Jewish Leadership Council said the petition 'provides no credible evidence' and drew on tropes widely recognised as antisemitic, and asked for its removal, which was refused; the Cabinet Office said it did not support a public inquiry but that the Prime Minister had asked the Ethics and Integrity Commission to review lobbying, disclosure and access.

pm9_world.topic: Europe, Canada, Australia and the Global South

claims.text: ELNET, founded 22 October 2007 and registered in Belgium, France, Germany, Poland, the UK, Italy and Israel, calls itself 'the most influential pro-Israel advocacy organisation in Europe'; its US arm, Friends of ELNET, launched in 2012 with nearly $1M from StandWithUs, raised more than $9.1M in 2023, and has received at least $11M from more than 100 US foundations and charities since 2022; co-founder Raanan Eliaz is a former AIPAC consultant; it has taken about 300 policymakers on trips to Israel and credits itself with Germany's approval of the $3.5B Arrow 3 purchase.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Canada) lobbied or took on Israel trips 156 of 269 MPs (58%) running in 2025, lobbying them 579 times since 2008 and spending $678,277 on their trips since 2007; Canada's Lobbying Commissioner wrote in May 2023 that sponsored travel 'could reasonably be seen to create a sense of obligation', and the Lobbyists' Code was changed that month to bar lobby groups from sponsoring travel for officials they lobby.
The Australia/Israel and Jewish Affairs Council runs the Rambam program taking federal politicians to Israel; a 2012 delegation included six Coalition MPs and senators.

The Israel Allies Foundation's parliamentary caucus network, begun with the Knesset Christian Allies Caucus in 2004, reached 50 countries and about 1,200 parliamentarians with Honduras in December 2020, describing its approach as 'faith-based diplomacy'; it linked new caucuses to embassy moves to Jerusalem by Honduras and Guatemala.

Israel was Guatemala's largest supplier of weapons, training and surveillance technology in the 1980s, after the US cut military aid in 1977; analysts tied Guatemala's 2018 embassy move to that history, to its president's evangelical base, and to its dependence on US aid and goodwill.

The African Union Commission chair granted Israel observer status in 2021; after an Israeli diplomat was removed from the AU summit in February 2023 the status was suspended pending a committee; South Africa had protested the grant, and Israel accused 'extremist states like Algeria and South Africa'.

The Israel Allies Foundation, founded in 2007 from the Knesset Christian Allies Caucus (2004) and Congressional Israel Allies Caucus (2006), reported 2018 revenue of $1,441,818; named US donors include Moskowitz family foundations ($760,000, 2009–13); it received money from Concert, an Israeli nonprofit with government matching funds, which the Forward said raised a FARA question; named affiliates include the Philippines, South Korea, Japan, Brazil, South Africa, Malawi, Australia, Canada and the European Parliament; it lobbies for anti-BDS laws and embassy moves to Jerusalem.

In 2020 the IAF network added caucuses in Cameroon, the Central African Republic and South Sudan; IAF president Josh Reinstein called the network 'the greatest tool that Israel has in its diplomatic arsenal'.
Netanyahu told Israel's envoys to Africa that his first interest was to 'dramatically change the situation regarding African votes at the UN' and to change their voting patterns.
According to SIPRI estimates for 2019–2023, the US supplied 69% of Israel's arms imports and Germany about 30%; US military aid exceeds $3 billion a year.

SIPRI: in 2019–2023 Israel was the 9th largest arms exporter (2.4% of world exports); India took 37% of Israel's exports, the Philippines 12% and the US 8.7%; Israel supplied 28% of the Philippines' imports and 11% of Morocco's.
